strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with asymptotic validity (Theorem 4.1) and power guarantees (Theorem 4.2) for the test statistic
Principled derivation of bi-level optimization formulation from Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, elegantly connecting kernel methods with spectral representation learning
Well-motivated problem addressing fundamental challenges in CI testing (Shah & Peters no-free-lunch result) with clear practical examples
Comprehensive technical analysis with detailed proofs; non-trivial extension of Kostic et al. (2024) to partial covariance operators
Concrete, implementable algorithm with thoughtful design choices (orthonormality regularization, whitening post-processing)
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only synthetic data on single model, no real data, no timing/scalability analysis, no evidence of practical advantage over KCIT/RCIT/GCIT despite scalability claims

Critical gap between theory and practice: Theory assumes E_m → 0 but provides no convergence rates, finite-sample bounds, or analysis of Algorithm 1 convergence; whitening post-processing not covered by theoretical guarantees
Strong unjustified assumptions: Assumption 4.1 (sub-Gaussianity of learned features) is assumed but never empirically verified; Assumption 3.1 sufficient conditions are non-trivial

Missing practical guidance: No principled method for selecting d, no hyperparameter selection guidance, no analysis of sample complexity m needed to achieve target E_m, no computational complexity analysis

Algorithm complexity concerns: Bi-level optimization with competing objectives (orthonormality regularization vs. main loss), suggesting suboptimal solutions requiring post-hoc whitening; unknown sensitivity to network architecture and hyperparameter choices

Asymptotic theory with restrictive conditions: Theorems are asymptotic only; regime d = o(√n) is limiting; power bound ε²_n ≥ 2dE²_m + cd²+log(δ⁻¹)/n can be stringent for weak signals, especially with non-negligible E_m
Limited novelty: Core spectral representation learning approach closely follows Kostic et al. (2024); main contribution is bi-level extension to partial covariance, which is somewhat incremental
